name: Executive Communication and Stakeholder Management
description: Board and investor updates, writing for executives, translating technical risk, stakeholder management, status reporting, meetings and presenting, negotiation, difficult conversations, crisis and client communication, influence and change communication.

cards.subject: BLUF
says: puts the conclusion or request in the first lines of a message
lets a busy reader act without finishing the message
is short for bottom line up front
cards.use: need the reader to know the ask from the opening sentence
not: saves the conclusion for the end to build suspense

cards.subject: Pyramid principle
says: leads with the answer and supports it with grouped arguments
builds a hierarchy in which each group of points sits under one governing idea
expects the points in each group to be the same kind of thing
cards.use: need to structure a long argument so the reader sees the answer and then the reasons
not: orders the arguments from weakest to strongest

cards.subject: One-page memo
says: limits an idea to a single page
forces the author to cut everything the decision does not need
is a common way to brief a senior reader before a conversation
cards.use: must brief a senior reader who will give it five minutes
not: is complete only when every supporting table is attached in the body

cards.subject: Executive summary
says: condenses a whole document into a section that can stand alone
is written last even though it appears first
states the recommendation, the reason and the decision needed
cards.use: want a reader to grasp a long report without opening it
not: is a table of contents with page numbers

cards.subject: Action subject line
says: states the needed action and deadline in the subject of an email
lets the reader sort the inbox by what needs a response
looks like Decision needed by Friday followed by the topic
cards.use: send an email that must not be mistaken for background reading
not: repeats the sender's name and the date

cards.subject: So-what test
says: asks of each paragraph why this reader should care
removes facts that change no decision for the audience
turns a finding into a consequence
cards.use: review a draft that lists findings without saying what they mean
not: checks the draft for spelling and grammar

cards.subject: Numbers with context
says: pairs each figure with a comparison such as target, prior period or benchmark
stops a lone number from being read in the most flattering way
shows direction as well as size
cards.use: quote a metric that means nothing on its own
not: rounds every figure to the nearest thousand

cards.subject: Calibrated confidence
says: states how sure the author is and what would change the conclusion
replaces blanket hedging with one clear statement of uncertainty
separates what is known from what is estimated
cards.use: must present a forecast that may turn out wrong
not: adds maybe and perhaps to every sentence to stay safe

cards.subject: Decision document
says: frames a choice with options, a recommendation and the decision needed
names the decider and the date by which the decision is needed
gives a senior reader what they need to say yes or no
cards.use: need a leader to choose between options
not: records what was decided after the fact only

cards.subject: Request for comments
says: circulates a proposal for written feedback before work begins
invites objections from peers across teams
makes disagreement visible while a change is still cheap
cards.use: want broad technical input on a proposal before building it
not: asks the approver for a signature without discussion

cards.subject: Architecture decision record
says: captures one decision with its context and consequences in a short dated file
lives next to the code as history for future engineers
is superseded by a later record when the decision changes
cards.use: want future engineers to learn why a design choice was made
not: lists every task of a project

cards.subject: Six-page narrative
says: replaces slides with a prose document read in silence at the start of the meeting
forces complete sentences and so exposes weak reasoning
makes the whole room start with the same information
cards.use: want a meeting to debate a complex proposal rather than watch a presentation
not: is a slide deck printed on six pages

cards.subject: Press release and FAQ
says: describes a product as if it had launched, before it is built
includes the hardest customer and internal questions with answers
works backwards from the customer benefit
cards.use: want to test whether a product idea can be explained as a clear customer benefit
not: is published to customers on the day work starts

cards.subject: Non-goals section
says: lists what a proposal will deliberately not do
heads off scope arguments before they start
tells reviewers which objections are out of scope
cards.use: are asked to keep expanding a proposal beyond its purpose
not: names the goals that are most likely to be missed

cards.subject: DACI
says: names a driver, an approver, contributors and informed people
gives each decision exactly one approver
is an acronym used to settle who decides
cards.use: find that a decision keeps stalling because nobody knows who decides
not: gives every contributor an equal vote

cards.subject: Two-way door decision
says: can be reversed cheaply, so it should be made quickly by a small group
contrasts with a one-way door that needs more review
scales the amount of approval to how hard reversal would be
cards.use: must decide how much process a choice deserves
not: always requires board approval

cards.subject: Board update
says: reports progress against plan to the directors
mixes headline metrics, wins, risks and requests for help
is sent on a regular schedule
cards.use: must report company progress to directors
not: is a transcript of the last leadership meeting

cards.subject: Board pre-read
says: circulates materials several days before the meeting
moves meeting time from presenting to discussion
is written to be understood without a presenter
cards.use: want directors to spend the meeting on decisions rather than slides
not: is handed out at the start of the meeting

cards.subject: No-surprises rule
says: tells directors significant bad news before the meeting
protects trust between management and the board
applies most when a problem will change the plan
cards.use: learn of a serious problem a week before the board meets
not: waits until the formal agenda item

cards.subject: Investor update
says: is a periodic note to investors with metrics, highlights and lowlights
is sent on a steady cadence whether the news is good or bad
is how investors are kept informed between board meetings
cards.use: want investors to stay informed without calling each of them
not: is sent only when the company raises money

cards.subject: Asks section
says: lists specific requests of the board or investors
names who could help and what exactly is needed
turns a passive report into an offer investors can act on
cards.use: want investors to introduce you to customers or candidates
not: thanks investors for their time

cards.subject: Lowlights
says: states what went wrong next to what went well
builds credibility because bad news is not left to be discovered
includes the cause and the plan to fix it
cards.use: are tempted to leave a missed target out of an investor note
not: moves bad news to the last page of the appendix

cards.subject: Variance explanation
says: explains the gap between plan and actual with cause and action
separates timing differences from real shortfalls
states whether the full-year outlook changes
cards.use: miss a quarterly target and must tell the board why
not: restates the number that was missed

cards.subject: Selective disclosure risk
says: arises when material non-public information goes to some investors and not others
can breach fair-disclosure rules at a public company
is reduced by sharing news with everyone at the same time
cards.use: consider sharing unreleased results with a favoured investor
not: only applies to private companies

cards.subject: Business impact framing
says: expresses a technical problem as effect on revenue, customers or compliance
replaces system names with consequences the listener cares about
answers what happens to the business if the risk occurs
cards.use: must explain a database weakness to a finance leader
not: lists the technical details in full

cards.subject: Likelihood and impact
says: rates a risk by how probable it is and how bad the effect would be
underlies the familiar risk matrix
lets unlike risks be ranked on one page
cards.use: need to rank a set of different risks
not: measures only the cost of the fix

cards.subject: Risk register
says: tracks each risk with an owner, a rating and a mitigation
is reviewed on a regular cadence
shows leaders the full list of known risks in one place
cards.use: need leaders to see every known risk with an owner
not: records only the risks that have already occurred

cards.subject: Risk appetite
says: states how much risk the organisation will accept to reach its goals
is set by leadership or the board, not by the team
gives engineers a basis to judge whether a risk needs escalation
cards.use: cannot tell whether a risk is small enough to accept
not: is the number of risks in the register

cards.subject: Cost of delay
says: puts a price on each week a piece of work is deferred
helps compare projects by value lost through waiting
turns a vague urgency into a figure
cards.use: need to show why waiting on a project is not free
not: is the cost of building the project

cards.subject: Recovery time objective
says: states the longest outage the business can tolerate
turns resilience into a number of minutes or hours
drives how much is spent on failover
cards.use: are asked how long customers might be without service
not: states how much data may be lost

cards.subject: Recovery point objective
says: states how much recent data the business can afford to lose
is measured as time back to the last good copy
drives how often backups or replication must run
cards.use: are asked how much data could vanish in a failure
not: states how fast service must come back

cards.subject: Pre-mortem
says: imagines that the plan has already failed and writes down why
surfaces concerns people hesitate to raise in a normal review
happens before commitment rather than after the event
cards.use: want a team to name its fears about a plan before launch
not: reviews what went wrong after a failure

cards.subject: Residual risk
says: is the risk that remains after controls are applied
must be knowingly accepted by someone with authority
is what a leader signs for when a mitigation is incomplete
cards.use: have applied controls and still see exposure
not: is the risk before any control exists

cards.subject: Stakeholder map
says: lists the people and groups affected by or able to affect the work
records what each needs and how they feel about the plan
is the starting point of a communication plan
cards.use: start a project that crosses many teams
not: is an organisation chart of one department

cards.subject: Power-interest grid
says: plots stakeholders by influence and interest
sorts people into manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed and monitor
helps choose how much effort each person deserves
cards.use: have too many stakeholders to treat equally
not: scores each person's performance

cards.subject: RACI
says: marks each person responsible, accountable, consulted or informed
expects one accountable person per task
clears up who does the work and who signs it off
cards.use: find two teams each assuming the other owns a task
not: gives every participant equal authority

cards.subject: Communication plan
says: lists audience, message, channel, frequency and owner
stops updates from depending on whoever remembers
matches the depth of each update to its audience
cards.use: need to keep many groups informed on a long project
not: is a single announcement email

cards.subject: Expectation management
says: agrees in advance what will be delivered, when and with what confidence
corrects a mismatch early rather than at the deadline
aligns what the sponsor expects with what the plan will deliver
cards.use: see that a sponsor's picture of the result differs from the plan
not: means promising less than the plan can deliver in every case

cards.subject: Stakeholder interview
says: is an early one-to-one conversation about needs and concerns
uncovers objections before they surface in a meeting
asks what success looks like for the other person
cards.use: are new to a programme and need to learn what matters to each group
not: is a survey sent to all staff

cards.subject: Pre-wiring
says: tests a proposal with key people one-to-one before the meeting
lets objections be handled in private
means that the meeting confirms support rather than creates it
cards.use: are about to present a controversial proposal to a group
not: circulates the deck for the first time during the meeting

cards.subject: Managing up
says: learns the boss's priorities and gives them what they need to decide
brings options and a recommendation, not only problems
avoids surprising the boss
cards.use: want a manager to trust your judgement and back your work
not: means asking the manager to solve each problem

cards.subject: Managing sideways
says: builds working relationships with peers who have no authority over you
trades help and information to reach shared goals
depends on understanding peers' own targets
cards.use: need another team's cooperation on a shared deadline
not: means going to their manager first

cards.subject: Silent stakeholder
says: holds real power but says little in meetings
must not be assumed to agree because they stay quiet
should be asked directly for their view outside the meeting
cards.use: notice that the finance director has not spoken on a plan that needs their budget
not: is a stakeholder who has approved the plan

cards.subject: RAG status
says: reports health as red, amber or green
gives a quick signal of whether intervention is needed
depends on shared criteria to mean the same thing everywhere
cards.use: want to flag at a glance which projects need attention
not: measures the budget spent to date

cards.subject: RAG criteria
says: are written thresholds that define each colour
keep red and amber from depending on who reports
say for example how many weeks of slip turns green to amber
cards.use: find that every project manager uses a different idea of amber
not: are the colours a sponsor prefers

cards.subject: Progress, plans, problems
says: is a three-part weekly update of done, next and blocked
fits on a single screen
gives readers a stable place to look for trouble
cards.use: want a short repeatable format for a weekly update
not: is a long report written monthly

cards.subject: Watermelon reporting
says: shows green on the outside and red inside
hides real problems behind optimistic status
grows when reporting a problem is punished
cards.use: notice that a project stays green until the day it fails
not: is a method of colouring reports by region

cards.subject: Exception reporting
says: reports only the items outside agreed tolerance
saves senior readers from details that are on track
relies on set thresholds for what counts as an exception
cards.use: need to keep a sponsor informed without long updates
not: reports every task every week

cards.subject: Burn-up chart
says: plots work completed against a line for total scope
shows scope changes as movement in the target line
lets readers see whether the finish date is slipping because of scope or pace
cards.use: need to show a sponsor that added scope, not slow work, moved the date
not: shows only the work remaining

cards.subject: Leading indicator
says: is a measure that predicts later results
gives early warning before an outcome is visible
contrasts with lagging measures such as revenue
cards.use: want a warning of trouble before it shows up in results
not: reports results that have already happened

cards.subject: Bad-news structure
says: states the problem, impact, cause so far, plan and request in order
is delivered as soon as the problem is known
brings a recommended path rather than only the problem
cards.use: must report a delay to a sponsor
not: waits until a full solution is ready

cards.subject: Date range forecast
says: gives a completion date as a range with a probability
replaces a single date that implies certainty
moves as new information arrives
cards.use: are asked for a firm date on work with open unknowns
not: promises the date the sponsor wants

cards.subject: Agenda with desired outcomes
says: states for each item what must be decided or learned
lets people judge whether they need to attend
turns topics into results to be reached
cards.use: are planning a meeting and want it to end with something concrete
not: lists topic names only

cards.subject: Timeboxing
says: gives each agenda item a fixed number of minutes
forces the group to decide when time runs out
protects later items from an overrunning early one
cards.use: see the first topic eating the whole hour
not: extends the meeting until all topics are done

cards.subject: Facilitator
says: runs the process of the meeting rather than the content
keeps to time and balances who speaks
is often a neutral person, not the most senior voice
cards.use: need a contested meeting to stay fair and on track
not: makes the final decision for the group

cards.subject: Parking lot
says: holds off-topic items for later
keeps an off-topic point on record without dismissing the speaker
needs an owner who follows up on parked items
cards.use: hear a valid point that does not belong to the current item
not: is where rejected ideas are discarded

cards.subject: Decision recap
says: ends a meeting by restating what was decided and who does what
catches misunderstandings while everyone is still present
feeds the written notes sent afterward
cards.use: are in the last minutes of a meeting and want to avoid later disputes
not: lists everything that was discussed

cards.subject: Action item with owner
says: assigns one named person and a date to a follow-up task
avoids the vague we will look into it
is the unit of accountability recorded in meeting notes
cards.use: want a follow-up to survive past the meeting
not: assigns the task to the whole team

cards.subject: Round-robin
says: asks each person in turn for their view
draws out quieter participants
reduces the weight of the loudest voice
cards.use: notice that two people dominate the discussion
not: lets whoever speaks first decide

cards.subject: Action title
says: writes a slide title as a full-sentence conclusion
lets a reader follow the story from titles alone
replaces a topic label such as Q3 revenue
cards.use: want slides to carry the argument by themselves
not: labels the slide with a one-word topic

cards.subject: Situation, complication, resolution
says: opens with shared context, then the problem, then the answer
is a way to frame a short presentation or memo
gives the listener a reason to care about the answer
cards.use: must open a presentation to a group who do not yet see the problem
not: starts with the solution only

cards.subject: Q&A preparation
says: lists the hardest likely questions with short answers
reduces the chance of being surprised in front of leaders
includes the question you hope nobody asks
cards.use: expect pointed questions from a board or customer
not: assumes that questions will not come

cards.subject: Deliberate pause
says: uses a short silence to emphasise a point
replaces filler words such as um
gives listeners a moment to take in what was said
cards.use: notice that you fill gaps with filler words
not: speeds up to finish sooner

cards.subject: BATNA
says: is your best alternative to a negotiated agreement
sets the lowest deal worth accepting
grows stronger when you develop other options before talking
cards.use: enter a negotiation and need to know when to walk away
not: is the first offer you make

cards.subject: Reservation point
says: is the least favourable deal you would still accept
is derived from your alternatives
should never be disclosed to the other side
cards.use: need a number below which you will not agree
not: is the opening offer

cards.subject: Zone of possible agreement
says: is the range where both sides' acceptable deals overlap
does not exist when the reservation points do not meet
is where a negotiated deal can fall
cards.use: find that the buyer's ceiling is below your floor
not: is the opening gap between offers

cards.subject: Anchoring
says: sets a reference point with the first number named
pulls later offers toward that number
is countered by naming your own anchor or reframing
cards.use: want to shape where a price discussion will land
not: is the practice of splitting the difference

cards.subject: Principled negotiation
says: separates people from the problem
focuses on interests, options for mutual gain and objective criteria
is associated with the book Getting to Yes
cards.use: want an agreement that keeps the relationship intact
not: wins by applying maximum pressure

cards.subject: Interests versus positions
says: treats a position as what someone says and an interest as why
looks for the need behind a demand
opens more solutions than arguing over positions
cards.use: are stuck because both sides repeat the same demand
not: means holding firm on the stated demand

cards.subject: Objective criteria
says: settle a disagreement by reference to an independent standard such as market rate
take the contest of wills out of a negotiation
give both sides a fair reason to accept a number
cards.use: reach a deadlock on price and need a neutral yardstick
not: are the preferences of the stronger party

cards.subject: Logrolling
says: trades issues that each side values differently
creates value rather than dividing a fixed amount
gives up something cheap to you for something valuable to you
cards.use: find that the two sides rank the issues differently
not: splits each issue equally

cards.subject: Labeling
says: names the other party's emotion aloud
shows that you have heard the feeling behind the words
starts with phrasing such as it seems like
cards.use: sense frustration in a counterpart and want to defuse it
not: denies the feeling is present

cards.subject: Concession discipline
says: gives up something only in exchange for something
shrinks each concession so the pattern signals a limit
avoids making large early gives
cards.use: are pressed to cut price without receiving anything
not: makes the biggest concession first to build goodwill

cards.subject: Yes, if
says: declines a request by stating the condition under which it could be done
offers a path rather than a closed door
keeps the relationship while holding a limit
cards.use: must refuse a request but still want to help
not: agrees now and hopes to find time later

cards.subject: Trade-off framing
says: asks what should move out when something is added
makes the cost of a request visible to its owner
hands the priority choice back to the person who asked
cards.use: get a new urgent task with a full plan already in place
not: quietly absorbs the extra work

cards.subject: Capacity statement
says: shows current commitments to explain what can be taken on
turns a refusal into a fact about the plan
invites the requester to choose what to drop
cards.use: are asked to take on work that would break existing promises
not: claims to be too busy without detail

cards.subject: Situation, behaviour, impact
says: describes when it happened, what was done and the effect
keeps feedback to observable facts
is a common structure for feedback
cards.use: must give feedback that the person can act on
not: labels the person's character

cards.subject: Opening statement
says: states purpose and facts in the first minute of a difficult conversation
avoids an ambush by saying what the meeting is about
invites the other person to respond
cards.use: are about to start a hard conversation and want to set the tone
not: opens with small talk for ten minutes

cards.subject: Paraphrasing
says: restates the other person's point in your own words
confirms understanding before you reply
lowers heat by showing they were heard
cards.use: need to check that you understood a complaint
not: repeats their words as a challenge

cards.subject: Impact without intent
says: describes the effect of an action without guessing the motive
avoids a defensive reply to an accusation
uses phrasing such as when this happened, I felt
cards.use: want to raise a problem without accusing someone of bad intent
not: states the motive you assume

cards.subject: Cooling-off pause
says: delays a reply when emotions are high
prevents sending words that cannot be taken back
can be as short as a walk or a night
cards.use: draft an angry reply to a colleague's email
not: answers immediately to show confidence

cards.subject: Contrasting statement
says: says what you do not mean and then what you do
corrects a misreading of your intent
uses phrasing like I don't want X, I want Y
cards.use: see that the other person thinks you are criticising their competence
not: repeats the original criticism more firmly

cards.subject: Communications lead
says: owns messages to outsiders during an incident
frees responders from answering questions
speaks with one voice to customers and press
cards.use: find engineers answering customer messages while fixing an outage
not: leads the technical repair

cards.subject: Incident commander
says: coordinates the response and makes decisions
assigns roles so responders do not duplicate effort
does not need to be the best technical fixer
cards.use: find that ten people are working on an incident with no coordination
not: writes the customer messages

cards.subject: Status page
says: publishes service health to customers in one public place
reduces support contacts during an outage
is updated by the communications owner
cards.use: want customers to check for outage news without contacting support
not: is an internal list of tickets

cards.subject: Holding statement
says: acknowledges an issue before the facts are known
promises a time for the next update
avoids speculation about cause
cards.use: must say something before the cause is understood
not: names the cause as soon as it is guessed

cards.subject: Blameless postmortem
says: reviews an incident for causes and fixes without blaming individuals
asks how the system allowed the error
encourages honest accounts
cards.use: want people to tell the truth about what happened in an outage
not: names the engineer who caused it

cards.subject: Customer impact statement
says: describes what customers experience rather than the internal cause
uses terms like cannot log in
is the core of a message to affected users
cards.use: write a notice about a failing service for non-technical users
not: explains the fault in the code

cards.subject: Known, unknown, next steps
says: separates facts, open questions and the next action
avoids speculation under pressure
fits into a short update
cards.use: need to write an update when the cause is still unclear
not: fills the gaps with the most likely guess

cards.subject: Accountable apology
says: states what happened, the impact, ownership and the fix
avoids passive phrases such as mistakes were made
avoids if you were offended wording
cards.use: must apologise to customers after a data error
not: expresses regret without admitting responsibility

cards.subject: Regulatory notification clock
says: may start when the company becomes aware of a breach
sets a legal deadline for informing a regulator
is a reason to bring counsel into an incident early
cards.use: suspect that customer data was exposed in an incident
not: starts only when the postmortem is complete

cards.subject: Escalation path
says: is a defined route to higher levels when an issue is not resolved in time
states who is contacted at each step and after how long
is agreed with the client before it is needed
cards.use: want a stalled issue to reach someone with authority
not: is complaining to the client's boss without notice

cards.subject: Service level agreement
says: is a written commitment on service levels such as response time
often states a remedy when the level is missed
gives the client an objective test of performance
cards.use: need to settle what response time the client was promised
not: describes the colour scheme of the report

cards.subject: Statement of work
says: defines deliverables, timeline and price boundary for an engagement
is the reference when a scope dispute appears
protects both sides from vague assumptions
cards.use: face a client asking for work that was never agreed
not: sets the response time for support tickets

cards.subject: Expectation reset
says: tells the client early that a date or result will change and why
comes with a new commitment and a reason
is better received before the deadline than after
cards.use: know that a delivery will be late
not: waits and hopes to catch up

cards.subject: Acknowledge before solving
says: confirms you understand and own the issue before explaining
lowers tension before technical detail
is the first move in a complaint reply
cards.use: open a reply to an angry client
not: begins with the technical cause

cards.subject: Warm handoff
says: introduces the client to the next owner and briefs that person first
spares the client from repeating the story
keeps trust during a transfer
cards.use: must pass a client to another team
not: forwards the ticket with no context

cards.subject: Take it offline
says: moves a heated or detailed exchange out of the group channel
avoids a public argument with a client
is followed by a summary to the group
cards.use: see a client challenging you in front of their executives
not: ignores the challenge

cards.subject: Call before email
says: delivers serious news by voice first and follows with a written note
lets the client react and ask questions at once
avoids tone being misread in text
cards.use: must tell a client that a milestone has been missed
not: sends only a written message

cards.subject: Discovery question
says: is an open question that uncovers the client's problem
comes before any pitch
asks about goals, obstacles and cost of doing nothing
cards.use: meet a prospect and want to learn before presenting
not: is a closed question that confirms a feature

cards.subject: Mutual action plan
says: is a shared document of joint steps and dates to complete a deal
makes the buyer's internal steps visible
signals how committed the buyer is
cards.use: want to know whether a prospect is really moving to a decision
not: is an internal sales forecast

cards.subject: Reciprocity
says: makes people feel obliged to return a favour
explains why early help makes later requests easier
is one of Cialdini's principles of influence
cards.use: want to build goodwill with a team you will need later
not: says people agree because others do

cards.subject: Social proof
says: leads people to follow what peers are doing
is strengthened by naming similar teams that adopted an idea
is another of Cialdini's principles of influence
cards.use: want a sceptical team to adopt a new practice
not: says people return favours

cards.subject: Commitment and consistency
says: leads people to act in line with a small stand they have already taken
explains why a small yes can lead to a bigger one
can be used by asking for a small public commitment first
cards.use: want a reluctant group to take the first step on a change
not: is the obligation to repay a favour

cards.subject: Coalition building
says: recruits supporters to carry a proposal
gives a proposal visible backing before it is formally put
uses allies from several functions
cards.use: need support from several departments for a proposal
not: tests an idea privately with one person

cards.subject: Shared goal framing
says: ties a request to the other party's own goals
shows what they gain by helping
starts from their incentives, not yours
cards.use: need a busy team to prioritise your request
not: describes why the request matters to you

cards.subject: Pilot
says: tests an idea on a small scale to produce evidence
lowers the risk of saying yes
lets sceptics see results before a wider rollout
cards.use: face resistance to a new process that has not been tried
not: asks for full rollout on trust

cards.subject: Disagree and commit
says: lets people argue a decision fully, then support it once made
avoids silent resistance after the decision
requires that the decider hears the dissent first
cards.use: see a team quietly undermine a decision they lost
not: requires unanimous agreement before action

cards.subject: Trust equation
says: combines credibility, reliability and intimacy, divided by self-orientation
shows why seeming self-serving lowers trust
comes from the book The Trusted Advisor
cards.use: want to explain why a talented adviser is not trusted
not: is a formula for calculating contract value

cards.subject: Async-first
says: defaults to written updates that do not need live attendance
lets people in different time zones contribute
moves meetings to cases that need live discussion
cards.use: work with a team spread across many time zones
not: requires everyone online at the same hour

cards.subject: Overlap hours
says: are the shared hours when team members in different time zones are online
are used for live discussion
are scarce, so they are kept for conversation that needs them
cards.use: must schedule a call across several regions
not: are the hours when nobody works

cards.subject: High-context communication
says: relies on shared background, tone and implication
leaves much unsaid because the listener is expected to infer it
is typical of cultures that value relationships and harmony
cards.use: find that a colleague's polite hint was actually a refusal
not: spells out everything in explicit words

cards.subject: Low-context communication
says: puts the meaning in explicit words
values directness and clear statements
expects little to be left to inference
cards.use: work with colleagues who expect instructions to be spelled out
not: relies on hints and tone

cards.subject: Indirect feedback style
says: softens criticism so the listener reads between the lines
may leave a direct-style listener unaware there was a problem
needs a manager to check what the listener took away
cards.use: give feedback to a colleague from a culture that avoids open criticism
not: states every flaw in plain terms

cards.subject: Plain English for global readers
says: avoids idioms, sport metaphors and slang
uses short sentences and common words
helps non-native readers and translation tools
cards.use: write for readers in many countries who use English as a second language
not: uses phrases like ballpark and touch base

cards.subject: Power distance
says: describes how far people accept unequal power in an organisation
affects whether juniors challenge seniors openly
is a dimension from Hofstede's research
cards.use: find that a team never questions the lead even when they should
not: measures the physical distance between offices

cards.subject: Internal announcement
says: tells staff what is changing, why, what it means for them and where to ask
reaches everyone affected at the same time
comes from the leader closest to the decision
cards.use: must tell staff about a reorganisation
not: is a rumour that spreads among teams

cards.subject: What's in it for me
says: answers what each audience gains or loses from a change
is tailored to each group rather than written once
turns a company message into a personal one
cards.use: find that staff accept the logic of a change but do not act
not: is the company's profit forecast

cards.subject: Case for change
says: explains why the current state cannot continue
gives staff a reason to leave the familiar
uses evidence such as customer or market data
cards.use: are asked why the company must change at all
not: lists the new system's features

cards.subject: Cascade communication
says: has leaders brief managers first who then brief their teams
gives managers time to prepare before staff hear
can distort the message as it passes down
cards.use: are rolling out a message to a large organisation in layers
not: sends the same email to all staff with no preparation

cards.subject: Manager briefing pack
says: gives managers talking points, FAQ and escalation contacts before staff are told
prepares managers for hard questions
aims to keep messages consistent
cards.use: want managers ready for questions on the day of an announcement
not: is the all-staff announcement itself

cards.subject: Change curve
says: maps typical emotional responses as people absorb a change
shows that dips in morale are expected
helps leaders match support to where people are
cards.use: see that morale has dropped after a change was announced
not: measures the project budget

cards.subject: ADKAR
says: lists awareness, desire, knowledge, ability and reinforcement
finds the stage at which a person is stuck
is a model for individual change
cards.use: find that people know about a change but do not adopt it
not: is a framework for budget approval

cards.subject: Feedback loop
says: gives staff a route for questions and concerns during a change
uses channels such as pulse surveys and open sessions
shows leaders where the message was misunderstood
cards.use: want to learn how a change is landing
not: broadcasts the message one way

cards.subject: Same-time disclosure
says: tells all affected people at the same time
limits the grapevine of partial information
is used for news that affects jobs
cards.use: must announce a restructure that will affect some teams
not: tells favoured staff first

cards.subject: Change champions network
says: is a set of volunteers across teams who relay the message and surface concerns
gives leaders ground-level feedback
spreads adoption through peers
cards.use: want peers rather than executives to help adoption
not: is a steering committee of executives

qa.q: What does BLUF ask a writer to do?
qa.right: Put the conclusion or request first, then the supporting detail
wrong: Build suspense by saving the conclusion for the final paragraph
Open with a long summary of the background before the point
List all attachments at the top of the email
qa.why: Bottom line up front means the reader sees the answer first.

qa.q: What is a BATNA?
qa.right: Your best alternative if the negotiation produces no agreement
wrong: The first price you propose to the other side
The highest price the other side would pay
A clause that locks in the final terms
qa.why: BATNA stands for best alternative to a negotiated agreement.

qa.q: What is the main job of a meeting facilitator?
qa.right: To run the process, keep time and balance who speaks
wrong: To make the final decision on every item
To present all the content of the meeting
To take the notes and email them out
qa.why: A facilitator manages process, not content.

qa.q: What does the first number named in a negotiation do?
qa.right: It acts as an anchor that pulls later offers toward it
wrong: It has no effect on the final result
It fixes the final price
It shows the other side your walk-away point
qa.why: Anchoring sets the reference for the rest of the discussion.

qa.q: Why is a pre-read circulated before a board meeting?
qa.right: So directors arrive informed and meeting time goes to discussion and decisions
wrong: So the board can approve items without meeting
So management can avoid presenting any numbers
So directors can edit the figures before the meeting
qa.why: The pre-read moves information transfer out of the meeting.

qa.q: What does a blameless postmortem aim to do?
qa.right: Find how the system allowed the error and fix it without naming a culprit
wrong: Identify the engineer who caused the outage for discipline
Keep the details of the incident from customers
Confirm that the existing process was followed
qa.why: Blame discourages honest accounts.

qa.q: What does a holding statement do during an incident?
qa.right: Acknowledges the problem and promises the next update before the cause is known
wrong: Announces the root cause as soon as a theory forms
Blames a third-party supplier to protect the brand
Waits to say anything until the fix is deployed
qa.why: It buys time honestly without speculating.

qa.q: A manager says 'I don't want to criticise your work, I want us to ship safely.' Which technique is this?
qa.right: A contrasting statement that corrects a misreading of intent
wrong: A feedback sandwich
An anchor
A holding statement
qa.why: It states what you do not mean and what you do.

qa.q: Which statement about the pyramid principle is correct?
qa.right: Start with the answer and group the supporting arguments beneath it
wrong: Start with the data and let the reader draw the conclusion
Order the arguments from the weakest to the strongest
Give equal weight to every point regardless of grouping
qa.why: The answer sits at the top of the pyramid.

qa.q: Which of these is a leading indicator for a support team?
qa.right: The number of open customer escalations rising week on week
wrong: Last quarter's revenue
Total customers lost this year
Annual profit
qa.why: Leading indicators predict later results.

qa.q: What does the recovery point objective describe?
qa.right: How much recent data the business can afford to lose
wrong: How long an outage may last
How many staff are needed for recovery
How many backups are stored
qa.why: RPO is a data loss tolerance; RTO is a time tolerance.

qa.q: What does the recovery time objective describe?
qa.right: The longest outage the business can tolerate
wrong: The amount of data that can be lost
The cost of the failover site
The time to detect an incident
qa.why: RTO is the target time to restore service.

qa.q: What does 'disagree and commit' require?
qa.right: Arguing before the decision, then supporting it fully after the decider chooses
wrong: Waiting for every person to agree
Voting until the majority is happy
Staying silent in the meeting and complaining afterward
qa.why: It avoids silent resistance.

qa.q: According to the trust equation, what lowers trust?
qa.right: High self-orientation, where the adviser seems to serve themselves
wrong: Too many deliverables
A long track record
Frequent contact
qa.why: Self-orientation is the divisor.

qa.q: Which statement about a two-way door decision is correct?
qa.right: It can be reversed cheaply, so it should be made quickly
wrong: It always needs board approval
It cannot be undone once taken
It must be delayed until all risks are removed
qa.why: Reversibility sets how much review a choice deserves.

qa.q: You are a CTO. The board asks about a database that has no tested backup. Which framing is best?
qa.right: 'If this database fails, we could lose up to a day of orders and be offline for two days. A tested backup costs X and removes most of that risk.'
wrong: 'Our PostgreSQL replication lag is unmonitored and snapshots are untested.'
'It is probably fine; we have never had a failure.'
'The engineers are concerned, so I need a budget.'
qa.why: Boards decide on business impact and cost, not on system detail.

qa.q: A project has been green for months. Two weeks before launch the lead discovers a three-week slip. What should the lead do first?
qa.right: Tell the sponsor now with the impact, the options and a recommendation
wrong: Wait until the next steering meeting so the update looks planned
Try to recover the slip quietly and report only if it grows
Change the criteria so the status stays amber
qa.why: Bad news is worth most when early, with a plan.

qa.q: Your team is at full capacity. A senior colleague asks for a new analysis by Friday. What is the best reply?
qa.right: 'I can do it if we move the pricing review to next week. Which matters more?'
wrong: 'Sure, I will fit it in.'
'No, I am too busy.'
'I will try, but it might not be done.'
qa.why: Trade-off framing keeps the relationship and returns the priority choice.

qa.q: You must propose a controversial reorganisation at a leadership meeting. What do you do before the meeting?
qa.right: Speak privately with the key leaders to hear objections and adjust the proposal
wrong: Send the deck the evening before so nobody has time to object
Present it cold to see who objects
Ask the CEO to announce it as decided
qa.why: Pre-wiring removes surprises.

qa.q: A major customer's service has been down for two hours and the cause is unknown. What should the communications lead post?
qa.right: A short update that confirms the impact, says the cause is being investigated and gives the time of the next update
wrong: A guess at the cause so customers feel informed
Nothing until the root cause is confirmed
A statement that the customer's own systems are probably to blame
qa.why: Honest acknowledgement with a promised update keeps trust.

qa.q: A prospect's champion says they love your product, but no meetings with finance or security are booked. What is the most useful next step?
qa.right: Propose a mutual action plan that names finance and security steps and dates
wrong: Send a discount to speed up their decision
Wait for the champion to come back
Present the product again to the champion
qa.why: Missing committee members mean the deal is not yet real.

qa.q: You told a client a feature would ship on 1 March. On 20 February you know it will be late. What do you do?
qa.right: Call the client now, explain why, give a new date and send the details in writing
wrong: Wait until 1 March in case it ships after all
Send an email on 2 March
Ship a partial version and say nothing about the rest
qa.why: Early reset and a call before an email.

qa.q: You are about to give a board member critical feedback. What opening best sets the conversation up?
qa.right: State the purpose and the facts, then invite their view
wrong: Ask casual questions for ten minutes first
Start with the strongest accusation
Say 'Don't take this personally' and then criticise
qa.why: The opening statement avoids an ambush.

qa.q: Two engineers argue about the cause of an outage in a shared customer channel. What should the account manager do?
qa.right: Take the discussion offline and post a single agreed update to the customer
wrong: Let both continue so the client sees the effort
Post both theories so the customer decides
Ask the client to pick one
qa.why: Customers need one voice.

qa.q: A stakeholder with budget authority has said nothing in three meetings about your proposal. What should you do?
qa.right: Ask them directly for their view in a one-to-one conversation
wrong: Assume their silence means approval
Remove their section from the plan
Escalate to their manager
qa.why: Silence is information you do not yet have.

qa.q: You are leading a distributed team across four time zones and decisions keep slipping. Which change is likely to help most?
qa.right: Write decisions in a shared document with an owner and a deadline, and use live calls for the hard points
wrong: Add a daily all-hands call at a fixed time
Ask everyone to reply to long email chains
Reduce the team to one time zone
qa.why: Async decisions plus selective live time.

qa.q: A stakeholder tells you 'we'll look at it' about your proposal in a culture where that often means no. What is the wisest step?
qa.right: Ask a gentle, concrete question about what would make it workable, then follow up
wrong: Assume they agreed and start work
Press for a yes or no right away
Send a formal email asserting the decision
qa.why: Indirect refusals need exploration.

qa.q: Both you and a supplier want a deal but disagree on price. You each value delivery speed and volume differently. What approach could create value?
qa.right: Trade the terms each side values most, such as faster payment for a lower unit price
wrong: Split the price difference down the middle
Walk away immediately
Repeat your original price more firmly
qa.why: Logrolling creates value by trading unlike priorities.

qa.q: You are asked to give a single completion date for a project with three major unknowns. What is the best answer?
qa.right: A range with the confidence level and what would narrow it
wrong: The earliest date possible to show ambition
A date with 50 percent padding hidden inside
'I cannot say anything'
qa.why: Ranges convey uncertainty honestly.

qa.q: A new CEO wants to announce a reorganisation to staff tomorrow. Which preparation matters most?
qa.right: Brief managers first with talking points and an FAQ so they can answer questions on the day
wrong: Send the announcement to all staff first and brief managers later
Tell only the senior leaders
Announce it by email without managers present
qa.why: Managers carry the message.

qa.q: A client says 'This is unacceptable!' in an email about a late report. What should your reply open with?
qa.right: An acknowledgement that you understand the impact, followed by what you are doing
wrong: The technical reasons for the delay
A reminder of what the contract says
A request for them to calm down
qa.why: Acknowledge before solving.

qa.q: Your forecast for the quarter will miss by 12 percent. The board meets in three weeks. What should you do?
qa.right: Tell the board chair now, with the cause and the plan, before the meeting
wrong: Wait for the board meeting to present the miss
Adjust the forecast assumptions to look closer
Tell only the investors
qa.why: No-surprises rule.

qa.q: A peer team keeps ignoring your requests for an API change. You have no authority over them. What is the best first step?
qa.right: Learn their own goals and show how your request helps them reach those goals
wrong: Escalate to their manager at once
Repeat the request more forcefully
Do the work yourself without telling them
qa.why: Shared goal framing.

qa.q: You face a team that doubts a new process. What gives you the strongest evidence for a rollout?
qa.right: A small pilot with a clear measure and results shared with the sceptics
wrong: A mandate from the CEO
A longer presentation of the theory
A promise that it will work
qa.why: A pilot lowers the cost of saying yes.

qa.q: Your company suffered a data exposure on Monday. Counsel says a regulator might need notice. When should legal be involved?
qa.right: As soon as the exposure is suspected, because notification deadlines may already be running
wrong: After the postmortem
After the customer message has been sent
Only if a customer complains
qa.why: The regulatory clock may start at awareness.

qa.q: A project sponsor reads a long weekly report and still asks 'Are we on track?' What fix is best?
qa.right: Add RAG status with written criteria and a one-line reason at the top
wrong: Make the report longer with more detail
Replace it with a verbal update only
Remove the status so the sponsor reads the details
qa.why: Status should be glanceable and consistent.

qa.q: A director asks a hostile question in front of the whole board and you do not know the answer. What is the best reply?
qa.right: Say what you know, say what you do not, and commit to a specific follow-up date
wrong: Give your best guess confidently
Dismiss the question as out of scope
Blame a colleague for not preparing you
qa.why: Honest uncertainty with a commitment keeps credibility.

qa.q: Your team accepts that a change is needed, yet three months later the old process is back. Which ADKAR element was most likely missed?
qa.right: Reinforcement
wrong: Awareness
Desire
Knowledge
qa.why: Reinforcement keeps a change in place.

qa.q: A VP wants you to approve a risk that has no owner and no rating. What should you ask for first?
qa.right: An entry in the risk register with an owner, a rating and a mitigation
wrong: A longer technical report
A verbal assurance
A new vendor
qa.why: Risks need owners.

qa.q: A vendor demands you accept their price by tomorrow or lose the offer. Your alternative is an approved competitor at a slightly higher price. What does your BATNA tell you?
qa.right: You can resist the deadline pressure because you have an acceptable alternative
wrong: You must accept to avoid losing the deal
You should hide the competitor's existence
You should raise the vendor's price
qa.why: A strong BATNA reduces the power of a deadline.

qa.q: An engineer wants to write a 12-page proposal for a change that is easy to reverse. What guidance fits best?
qa.right: Treat it as a two-way door decision and decide quickly with a short note
wrong: Require full board approval
Write a six-page narrative
Postpone until all risks are removed
qa.why: Reversibility scales the process.

qa.q: A meeting is overrun by one topic, and the last two agenda items are at risk. What should the facilitator do?
qa.right: Stop the discussion, park the detail with an owner and move on
wrong: Let the discussion run until it ends
Drop the last two items without comment
Ask the senior person to decide immediately
qa.why: Timebox and park.

qa.q: Your engineering lead says 'it's 80% done' for the third week running. What is the best question for a status check?
qa.right: 'What specifically remains, and how confident are you in the date?'
wrong: 'Can you work faster?'
'Why do you keep saying 80%?'
'Is it green or red?'
qa.why: Ask for remaining work and confidence.

qa.q: An investor update is due and the month was poor. What approach builds the most credibility?
qa.right: Report the miss with its cause and plan alongside the wins, and include a specific ask
wrong: Skip the update this month
Report only the wins
Describe the miss in vague terms
qa.why: Lowlights build credibility.

qa.q: A customer asks for an apology after an outage. Which wording is best?
qa.right: 'We caused the outage, here is the impact on you, and here is what we changed.'
wrong: 'Mistakes were made.'
'We are sorry if you were inconvenienced.'
'The outage was caused by a third-party supplier.'
qa.why: Accountable apology.

qa.q: During a hard conversation the other person shouts. What is the most helpful move?
qa.right: Pause, acknowledge the strength of the feeling and agree a time to continue
wrong: Match their volume
Continue listing facts
End the relationship
qa.why: Cooling-off pause.

qa.q: Your manager keeps being surprised by problems you raise late. Which habit fixes this?
qa.right: Share issues early with options and a recommendation
wrong: Share only when the problem is solved
Send more detailed reports weekly
Escalate to the manager's boss
qa.why: Managing up means no surprises.

qa.q: A chat channel has 300 messages about a launch and no clear decision. What is the best step?
qa.right: Write a decision document naming the options, the recommendation, the decider and the date
wrong: Add more people to the chat
Start a daily stand-up
Ask someone to summarise at the end of the week
qa.why: The decision document makes the choice explicit.

qa.q: You are asked to explain a multi-region failover to a non-technical director. Which approach best serves them?
qa.right: State the business effect, use a simple comparison and give the cost of the options
wrong: List the technologies used
Give a full architecture diagram
Offer to send documentation
qa.why: Business impact framing.

qa.q: Your announcement of a policy change got many complaints that 'nobody told us'. What is the most likely fix?
qa.right: Repeat the message through several channels and give managers a briefing pack
wrong: Send the same email again once
Turn off replies
Change the policy
qa.why: Repetition and managers.

qa.q: Two teams each think the other owns a customer escalation. Which tool most directly prevents that?
qa.right: A RACI with one accountable owner per escalation
wrong: A longer meeting
A faster email system
A power-interest grid
qa.why: One accountable owner.

qa.q: Your English-language document will be read by teams in six countries, many of them non-native speakers. Which choice helps most?
qa.right: Use short sentences and avoid idioms
wrong: Add sports metaphors for engagement
Use long sentences for precision
Use abbreviations to save space
qa.why: Plain English.

qa.q: A salesperson is asked to quote a price in the first call. What is a sensible response?
qa.right: Ask discovery questions to learn the problem before naming a price
wrong: Name the lowest price to win trust
Name the highest price they can think of
Refuse to discuss price at all
qa.why: Learn before pricing.

qa.q: You proposed two options and a recommendation to the CEO who asked 'What do you need from me?' What is the best answer?
qa.right: One decision, by a date, with the consequence of delay
wrong: A long list of things the team would like
Nothing, just keep me informed
Whatever the CEO thinks best
qa.why: Be specific about the ask.

qa.q: At a board meeting you must present a metric that fell. Which presentation of the figure is best?
qa.right: The figure with prior period, target, cause and action
wrong: The figure alone
The figure after rounding up
The average of the last three years
qa.why: Numbers with context.

qa.q: A buyer asks you to match a competitor's lower price. What is the best move?
qa.right: Ask what else matters to them and trade a concession for something in return
wrong: Match the price at once
Refuse and end the call
Reveal your own minimum price
qa.why: Concession discipline.

qa.q: You need a sceptical CFO's support for a project. What approach is most likely to help?
qa.right: Frame the request in the CFO's goals, bring pilot evidence and ask for input on the plan
wrong: Escalate to the CEO
Present only the technical benefits
Wait for the CFO to approach you
qa.why: Shared goals and evidence.

qa.q: Leaders announce layoffs to affected people in groups on different days. What risk does this create?
qa.right: Partial information spreads through the grapevine before everyone hears
wrong: The announcement takes less time
Managers lose control of the schedule
Regulators get the notice late
qa.why: Same-time disclosure avoids the grapevine.

qa.q: You see a status report with ten bullet points and no conclusion. What is the quickest improvement?
qa.right: Add a one-line headline at the top stating status, the key risk and the ask
wrong: Add another bullet
Change the font
Send it to more people
qa.why: BLUF for status.

qa.q: A client's account lead tells you the sponsor is unhappy but wants to hear it from you. What should you do?
qa.right: Call the sponsor, listen, then confirm what you will do in writing
wrong: Send an email only
Wait for the next scheduled review
Ask the account lead to handle it
qa.why: Call first, follow up in writing.
